description: Our team brings a proven track record of tackling complex issues through innovative software design. We are a collective of passionate professionals who thrive on building technological systems with purpose. For us, engineering and medicine is never just theory—it is science in action. Drawing on our experience in bridging the gap between raw data and actionable software in real-time monitoring.
summary:
On long-duration space missions, astronauts must monitor their health while facing microgravity, radiation, isolation, and delayed communication with Earth. The challenge is not simply collecting measurements, but recognizing when changes across multiple physiological systems may matter.

Medivierse is an astronaut-centered health monitoring concept supported by an interactive software prototype. Its proposed platform integrates five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immunological, radiation exposure, and behavioral health. By organizing health indicators, self-reports, and mission context around individual baselines, Medivierse aims to reveal longitudinal trends, identify potential concerns, and support informed medical follow-up.

Grounded in NASA's Human Research Program and Spaceflight Standard Measures, our submission combines an interactive astronaut interface with documented monitoring workflows and a proposed cross-domain assessment architecture.

Medivierse envisions a future where astronauts can better understand their health, recognize meaningful changes, and make informed decisions alongside medical teams during missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
details:
Problem:

Human spaceflight presents a unique medical challenge. Astronauts experience physiological changes caused by microgravity, radiation exposure, altered circadian rhythms, and prolonged isolation. These conditions affect multiple systems simultaneously, from cardiovascular regulation and bone metabolism to immune function and cognitive performance.

During long-duration missions, particularly those beyond low Earth orbit, these risks become more difficult to manage. Medical resources are limited, communication with Earth may be delayed, and astronauts must increasingly participate in monitoring their own health.

NASA has generated extensive knowledge about these effects through its Human Research Program and spaceflight studies. However, translating measurements from different physiological systems into an accessible, individualized health assessment remains a challenge.

This is the problem we set out to address with Medivierse.

Solution:

Medivierse is a health monitoring software project designed to help astronauts understand their physiological status, identify potentially concerning changes, and maintain a structured record of their health throughout a mission.

Our approach brings together five complementary areas of space medicine.

Cardiovascular Health

We selected indicators including systolic and diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure, heart rate, ECG, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, and relevant laboratory measurements. These are intended to support monitoring of cardiovascular adaptation to microgravity, including fluid redistribution, hemodynamic changes, cardiac rhythm alterations, and orthostatic intolerance.

Musculoskeletal Health

The proposed assessment incorporates bone mineral density, DXA measurements, bone turnover biomarkers such as β-CTX and P1NP, and functional evaluations of muscle strength and physical performance. Longitudinal comparison is particularly relevant because changes in bone and muscle function develop progressively during spaceflight.

Immunological Health

We identified leukocyte counts and differentials, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, inflammatory markers such as CRP and IL-6, salivary cortisol, and indicators of latent viral reactivation. These parameters were selected based on research describing immune dysregulation, altered stress responses, and viral shedding during spaceflight.

Radiation Exposure

This component is designed to contextualize personal and cumulative radiation exposure, including risks associated with galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events. Radiation measurements would be considered alongside relevant biological observations, while distinguishing exposure itself from possible health effects.

Behavioral Health

The proposed system includes daily mood and fatigue assessments, sleep monitoring, cognitive vigilance testing, and standardized psychological questionnaires. Instruments considered in our research include PHQ-9, GAD-7, PSS-10, the Psychomotor Vigilance Test, and measures of social adaptation.

Together, these domains provide a broader view of astronaut health than individual measurements alone.

How Medivierse Works:

The proposed user experience begins with astronaut identification and mission configuration. The system is designed to retrieve available preflight measurements, previous assessments, and information relevant to the current mission phase.

The astronaut then completes a guided health check-in, either through written responses or a proposed voice-assisted interaction. The workflow includes questions about mood, stress, sleep, symptoms, and general well-being.

A central workspace is designed to present physiological information through an interactive human-body visualization, supported by numerical measurements and health summaries.

Behind this interface, our proposed assessment architecture follows four main processes:

1. Data collection and standardization. Physiological measurements, laboratory indicators, radiation records, and self-reported information are organized into a common structure. The design allows for both manual inputs and future integration with monitoring devices.

2. Individualized assessment. Current measurements are compared with available baseline information and previous observations. The architecture also specifies derived indicators, including mean arterial pressure, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and longitudinal changes in bone turnover biomarkers.

3. Trend detection and clinical alerts. The proposed rule-based assessment system distinguishes between expected findings, potential warnings, and situations requiring further evaluation. Missing measurements and uncertain findings are identified rather than treated as confirmed abnormalities.

4. Health summaries and follow-up. Results are intended to be presented in a format that astronauts can understand, with relevant trends, suggested follow-up assessments, and pathways for communication with medical personnel. The workflow also includes a dedicated emergency pathway.

An important part of the design is the relationship between different physiological indicators. For example, reduced sleep efficiency, increasing fatigue, and slower reaction times may be more informative when considered together. Similarly, changes in stress indicators and immune measurements may warrant further assessment without necessarily establishing a causal relationship.

The objective is to support medical decision-making, not automate clinical diagnoses.

Scientific Research and Development:

Our work began with a review of NASA research and peer-reviewed literature on the effects of spaceflight on human physiology.

We examined cardiovascular adaptation during long-duration missions, NASA's Biochemical Profile Project, Spaceflight Standard Measures, radiation-related health risks, salivary antimicrobial proteins, stress biomarkers, and immune changes observed in astronauts.

From this research, we identified physiological variables that could contribute to an integrated monitoring system. We then organized them into clinical assessment algorithms and developed flowcharts describing data entry, parameter evaluation, alert classification, and follow-up.

The proposed backend architecture includes data validation, calculation of derived indicators, assessment rules for each physiological domain, cross-domain trend analysis, and longitudinal health records.

Our current software implementation includes an interactive astronaut-facing interface developed with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and HTML5 Canvas. It features an immersive spacecraft-inspired environment, astronaut identification, simulated mission telemetry, and an interactive spacesuit visualization with physiological monitoring nodes.

The accompanying research and system design documentation establishes the broader monitoring workflow that we intend to implement beyond the current interface.

What Makes Medivierse Different?:

We designed Medivierse around a simple clinical principle: an astronaut's health cannot be understood through isolated measurements alone.

A blood pressure reading, a stress questionnaire, or an immune biomarker may provide useful information individually, but its significance also depends on the astronaut's baseline, previous measurements, mission conditions, and other physiological findings.

Medivierse therefore focuses on three elements: personalized baselines, longitudinal assessment, and integration across physiological systems.

This approach also recognizes that terrestrial clinical reference ranges cannot always be applied directly to spaceflight. Measurements must be interpreted in context, and any proposed clinical thresholds require appropriate validation.

Rather than introducing another collection of disconnected health indicators, our goal is to create a monitoring experience that helps astronauts understand how their health is changing and which findings deserve attention.

Potential Impact and Next Steps:

Medivierse is currently an interactive software prototype supported by a scientific research framework, clinical assessment algorithms, and a proposed technical architecture.

Our next development priorities include implementing the complete monitoring workflow, integrating suitable biomedical datasets, testing the assessment logic using clearly identified simulated scenarios, and refining the clinical rules with expert review.

Future versions could incorporate more automated data collection, longitudinal visualization, and structured communication with flight surgeons.

We recognize that medical decision-support software intended for space missions requires extensive verification and validation. Medivierse is not presented as a clinically validated diagnostic system.

Our goal is to contribute to a future in which astronauts have access to clearer, more personalized health information and can participate more effectively in monitoring their well-being during long-duration missions.

Medivierse brings together space medicine, biomedical research, and interactive software design to make astronaut health monitoring more integrated, understandable, and accessible.
